PERMA: Benchmarking Personalized Memory Agents via Event-Driven Preference and Realistic Task Environments

2018
Abstract.

Empowering large language models with long-term memory is crucial for building agents that adapt to users’ evolving needs. However, prior evaluations typically interleave preference-related dialogues with irrelevant conversations, reducing the task to needle-in-a-haystack retrieval while ignoring relationships between events that drive the evolution of user preferences. Such settings overlook a fundamental characteristic of real-world personalization: preferences emerge gradually and accumulate across interactions within noisy contexts. To bridge this gap, we introduce PERMA, a benchmark designed to evaluate persona consistency over time beyond static preference recall. Additionally, we incorporate (1) text variability and (2) linguistic alignment to simulate erratic user inputs and individual idiolects in real-world data. PERMA consists of temporally ordered interaction events spanning multiple sessions and domains, with preference-related queries inserted over time. We design both multiple-choice and interactive tasks to probe the model’s understanding of persona along the interaction timeline. Experiments demonstrate that by linking related interactions, advanced memory systems can extract more precise preferences and reduce token consumption, outperforming traditional semantic retrieval of raw dialogues. Nevertheless, they still struggle to maintain a coherent persona across temporal depth and cross-domain interference, highlighting the need for more robust personalized memory management in agents. Our code and data are open-sourced at https://github.com/PolarisLiu1/PERMA.

1. Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) (Jaech et al., 2024; Grattafiori et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2024) has catalyzed a shift from static knowledge access paradigms to interactive agents capable of sustained engagement (Zheng et al., 2025). In this new paradigm, long-term memory is no longer merely a tool for knowledge retrieval, but a prerequisite for maintaining coherent user representations across interactions. A reliable memory-equipped agent not only stores past information, but continuously constructs and updates a consistent persona state that reflects users’ constraints and behavioral tendencies over time (Hu et al., 2025).

Despite these requirements, inherent limitations in context window size and token costs present significant bottlenecks (Tavakoli et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a). To mitigate these challenges, recent progress in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Gao et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2025; Yue et al., ; Luo et al., 2025) has bolstered LLMs’ capacity to extract relevant factual knowledge (Zhu et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025). To further refine retrieval quality, several approaches have introduced structured memory indices (Xu et al., 2025c; Xu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a), such as tree- (Rezazadeh et al., 2024; Sarthi et al., 2024) and graph-based (Gutiérrez et al., 2025b; Chhikara et al., 2025; Wang and Chen, 2025a; Ma et al., 2024) representations. Complementing these retrieval techniques, reinforcement learning (RL) has been incorporated to optimize memory utilization in long-context settings (Yu et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026; Mao et al., 2026). Beyond generic storage mechanisms, personalization-oriented agents leverage modular memory architectures and context-aware memory structures. These agents emphasize capturing user profiles and preferences to inform downstream conditioning for long-horizon planning and lightweight deployment (Li et al., 2025c; Fang et al., 2025). While these architectural innovations endow agents with the potential for long-range memory, the method for quantifying their personalized performance within complex, noisy real-world scenarios remains an open challenge.

Along this line, empirical studies (Jiang et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025a) have underscored the inherent difficulties in verifying user-centric personalization, a task typically benchmarked by preference recall fidelity and robustness to token-level noise across extended interactions (Maharana et al., 2024). While current LLMs excel at factual retention (Wang et al., 2025a), effective personalization necessitates a paradigm shift (Gutiérrez et al., 2025a; Bian et al., 2026): treating user preferences not as static attributes, but as evolving behavioral patterns that must be contextually inferred and extracted during ongoing task interactions (Jiang et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2026). Thus, the primary bottleneck is not simple memorization, but the interpretation, integration, and retrieval of preference signals that are often latent, incrementally expressed, or obscured by conversational noise. Unfortunately, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a), existing evaluation frameworks remain insufficient for assessing the longitudinal consistency of persona understanding, due to three limitations: (1) Preference-Centric Framing: Existing protocols (Zhao et al., 2025a) construct the origins of preferences using static statements from a user perspective, rather than capturing the adaptive nature of preferences through iterative feedback. Such a formulation turns the conversation into a preference briefing, thereby overlooking how preferences manifest through event-driven dialogues. Consequently, the resulting evaluation ignores the interactive nuances of real-world deployment, failing to represent noise-rich scenarios such as ambiguous requests (Li et al., 2025b). (2) Static User Modeling: As preferences are predefined prior to dialogue, models are evaluated based on isolated user preferences (Zhao et al., 2025a; Feng et al., 2026), treating them as static snapshots and neglecting cross-session dependencies that are essential for assessing agents’ ability to reason over continuous interactions. It remains difficult to verify whether a model can achieve the cross-domain synthesis and retrieval required for complex queries (Jiang et al., 2025a), often leading retrieval-based approaches to appear effective under recall-oriented settings while their performance is overestimated (Wu et al., 2026). (3) Outcome Assessment: Ideally, a memory-augmented agent should progressively integrate interaction histories and user preferences to enhance the efficiency of subsequent sessions, thereby reducing token overhead and minimizing the need for redundant repetitive user prompting. Current evaluation paradigms primarily focus on the capabilities of long-context models and assess performance mainly based on the final LLM outputs, conflating memory retrieval with the generation process in memory systems rather than evaluating them separately. As a result, the quality and efficiency of the underlying memory systems, as well as memory utility in interactive scenarios, remain unexamined. These limitations highlight the need for alignment between preference benchmark construction and real-world interaction scenarios.

To this end, we introduce PERMA, a benchmark designed to evaluate the maintenance of persona states, defined as a combination of dynamic user preferences and episodic memory. PERMA models personalization as a temporally evolving state derived from interaction events, where each session addresses specific task requirements within a targeted topic. Through this process, fine-grained preference details are not explicitly given as standalone statements, but are inferred from how users articulate requests, provide feedback, and refine constraints across turns. These extracted preference signals, together with interaction history, are integrated into the evolving persona state, progressively enriching the user profile. As illustrated in Figure 1 (b), we construct the interaction histories of representative users across 10 countries and diverse age demographics, spanning over 20 distinct topics and extending the scope to include 2,166 preference details. As shown in Table 1, the corpus contains upwards of 800 events, with style-aligned contexts totaling 1.8M tokens. To ensure both structural coherence and linguistic realism, we adopt a two-stage generation process as illustrated in Figure 2. A timeline generation agent first transforms these events into detailed descriptions and objectives necessary for dialogue reconstruction. Events are categorized into “emergence” and “supplement” types to distinguish between the emergence of new preferences and the refinement of existing ones across different topics. Subsequently, a dialogue generation agent is prompted to flesh out the full conversation based on the event descriptions and objectives, yielding a Clean version with standard, non-rigid interactions. The agent also specifies the concrete preference being realized. To ensure coherence and consistency, we employ an LLM-based verification pipeline and human validation, triggering an iterative re-generation loop whenever preferences are not presented in the dialogue. Drawing on challenges from prior research, we incorporate two key factors to better approximate real-world interactions. First, we introduce text variability through the injection of five types of human prompt biases (Tian et al., 2025) into each event as in-session noise, thereby capturing realistic within-session disruptions such as intent shifts, ambiguous expressions, and preference corrections. Second, we model linguistic alignment with authentic data by aligning user queries with individual idiolects from WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024), fostering diverse phrasing patterns grounded in natural interactions. Finally, we construct three distinct context tiers for comparative analysis: Clean, In-session Noise, and Style-aligned Long-context. Table 2 provides illustrative examples of injected in-session noise types and style-aligned queries.

To conclude, PERMA enables us to investigate the impact of persona construction across multiple domains, natural prompting noise, and temporal evolution. To evaluate LLM agent behavior under these settings, we design multiple-choice questions (MCQs) from three perspectives, namely task completion, preference consistency, and information confidence, to examine whether agents can retrieve and apply historical information in one shot. Meanwhile, to simulate real-world multi-turn interaction, we further implement an LLM-based user simulator that provides supplemental information when preference is unmet. This creates an iterative feedback loop between the simulator and the LLM agent, which continues until the generated response satisfies the underlying preference. We benchmark a diverse set of standalone LLMs and agents equipped with memory systems, analyzing their effectiveness in contextualizing user preferences and retrieving relevant memory segments. Furthermore, we conduct probing evaluations at various temporal intervals along the dialogue timeline to examine how performance evolves as persona states accumulate and potentially drift. This comprehensive analysis offers critical insights into the underlying mechanics of memory systems and their capacity to sustain coherent persona states under realistic, long-term interaction conditions. Our contributions are summarized below:

  1. (1)

    We introduce a novel benchmark for evaluating LLM agents that shifts the paradigm from static preference matching to event-driven dialogue scenarios. Unlike existing frameworks, our benchmark incorporates realistic in-session noise and linguistic style to assess how well agents infer and extract preferences through natural, iterative interactions.

  2. (2)

    We formulate a dynamic user modeling evaluation protocol that tests an agent’s ability to maintain and update persona states. By focusing on cross-session dependencies and cross-domain synthesis, our framework evaluates the agent’s capacity to reason over continuous interactions, rather than merely recalling isolated facts.

  3. (3)

    We design a comprehensive assessment suite across multiple dimensions. By employing a user simulator to facilitate multi-turn interactions and incorporating temporal probing, we assess how models synthesize and apply memory over evolving persona states, revealing their strengths and limitations under temporal drift and semantic interference.

2. Related Work

2.1. Evolution of Personalization Memory Benchmarks

2.1.1. Evaluating Long-Context Memory Capabilities of LLMs

The evaluation of long-context capabilities in LLMs (Wang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025; Yen et al., 2025) has historically relied on “Needle-in-a-Haystack” style tests that measure a model’s ability to retrieve facts embedded within lengthy contexts (OpenAI et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023). While early benchmarks were limited to 10k-token interactions, recent efforts (Maharana et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025b; Tavakoli et al., 2026), such as LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) extend evaluation to ultra-long multi-session dialogues ranging from 115k to over 1.5M tokens, incorporating tasks that probe cross-session memory and free-form question answering. Nevertheless, these benchmarks primarily evaluate whether models can access and reason over long interaction histories, rather than how user preferences are incrementally inferred and integrated during ongoing interactions for personalization. Table 3 provides a comparison between existing memory and personalization evaluations across multiple dimensions.

2.1.2. Towards Personalization in Memory

At the core of personalized interaction and lifelong digital companions (Wu et al., 2026) lies the concept of user preferences (Zhang et al., 2025b; Ren et al., 2019; Du et al., 2024), defined as the longitudinal collection of a user’s stable interests, stylistic inclinations, and task-specific constraints (He et al., 2026). For a personalized agent (Li et al., 2025a; Xu et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026b), these preferences constitute a latent state that must be captured from historical interactions to guide subsequent response generation. This ensures that agent behavior aligns with individual expectations without necessitating repetitive, explicit instructions. The fundamental necessity of preference modeling is to alleviate the “interaction burden” — empowering agents to proactively anticipate user needs from historical context, thereby enhancing efficiency and user satisfaction in real-world applications.

Broadly, personalization benchmarks have evolved from (i) static preference conditioning to (ii) multi-session preference retention, yet few explicitly evaluate whether models can maintain a coherent persona state under evolving, information-dense interactions. Early frameworks, such as PrefEval (Zhao et al., 2025a) and PerLTQA (Du et al., 2024), characterized personalization as conditional response generation, focusing on an LLM’s capacity for long-context understanding, user modeling and adherence to a constrained set of stated preferences. These studies revealed that contemporary LLMs struggle to infer implicit preferences accurately and apply them consistently across conversational turns, particularly when intervening dialogues introduce unrelated topics as “contextual token noise” (Tan et al., 2025a). Despite these advancements, it remains designed for “Needle-in-a-Haystack” tasks, in which isolated preferences are retrieved from vast volumes of unrelated context. To enhance the recognition of personalized intent, UserBench (Qian et al., 2025a) and PersonaLens (Zhao et al., 2025b) introduced interactive, gym-like environments. These benchmarks advanced the field toward simulating real-world agent dynamics; however, they treat user profiles as fixed inputs rather than evolving constructs. A pivotal shift toward memory retention occurred with PersonaMem (Jiang et al., 2025a), which incorporated multi-session interaction histories. PersonaMem centers on preference-driven dialogue construction; consequently, its dialogues resemble subjective opinion sharing rather than objective problem solving. Subsequently, PersonaMem-v2 (Jiang et al., 2025b) further advances this paradigm by focusing on implicitly expressed preferences and requiring LLMs to infer user traits from subtle conversational nuances. It assumes that implicit behavioral cues can be consistently abstracted into stable preference variables. However, in realistic interactions, many implicit signals are situational and do not necessarily correspond to enduring persona states. These frameworks still evaluate preference recognition and recall within constructed interaction traces, without explicitly probing the stability, cross-domain synthesis, and temporal consistency of the underlying persona state. Recent efforts, such as the KnowMe-Bench (Wu et al., 2026), use long-form narratives as a data substrate to evaluate evidence-grounded inference about motivation, identity development, and psychological states. Yet KnowMe-Bench is better characterized as a narrative-reasoning benchmark rather than as an assessment of personalized conversational user-assistant interaction or dialogue management.

To address these limitations, PERMA introduces a dynamic evaluation paradigm centered on active dialogue management. We shift the evaluative focus from single-point preference recall to composite synthesis, requiring memory systems to integrate interdependent traits across information-dense sessions to resolve complex queries. By employing an event-driven methodology, our framework captures the evolutionary nature of user profiles; specifically, the interplay between newly emerged and updated preferences, while moving beyond “black-box” long-context reasoning evaluation through a decoupled assessment of retrieved memory quality and generative reasoning. As a result, PERMA reframes personalization evaluation from preference identification to persona state maintenance across temporally ordered events with structured noise and cross-domain dependencies. Such requirements extend beyond traditional dialogue retrieval, motivating the development of dedicated memory systems and memory-enabled agents for persistent user modeling.

2.2. From Static Retrieval to Persistent Memory

Personalization in LLMs has undergone a fundamental architectural shift driven by the growing mismatch between transient context conditioning and the requirements of long-term user–assistant relationships (Xu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2024). Early approaches implicitly equated personalization with prompt augmentation, assuming that user history could be sufficiently represented within a fixed or expanded context window. However, this assumption fails at scale: attention-based architectures exhibit context dilution and the “lost-in-the-middle” phenomenon, rendering long-term user modeling inefficient (Liu et al., 2023).

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) (Gao et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2025; Gutiérrez et al., 2025a) reframed this problem by externalizing memory into non-parametric storage. By enabling semantic access to large repositories of user-related information, RAG alleviated context window constraints and improved factual grounding. Yet this architectural move introduced a new limitation: memory was reduced to static, document-like artifacts retrieved reactively based on semantic similarity (Li et al., 2025b; Qian et al., 2025b). In doing so, RAG systems remain inherently stateless, primarily serving as indexing mechanisms for user-assistant dialogue rather than modeling the temporal evolution and coherence of user personas (Neelakanteswara et al., 2024).

Unlike passive retrieval in vanilla RAG, agentic frameworks utilize LLMs as reasoning engines to orchestrate tool use (Wang et al., 2025c; Yuan et al., 2025) and multi-step planning (Zhang et al., 2025c). However, for an agent to exhibit consistent personality and long-term adaptation, it requires a persistent memory system, which functions as the agent’s long-term storage. Recent work (Zhang et al., 2024; Du, 2026; Xu et al., 2025d; Wang and Chen, 2025b) has begun to formalize this transition by treating memory as a structured, lifecycle-aware subsystem. Rather than storing immutable embeddings, memory architectures introduce mechanisms for consolidation, reinforcement, decay, and reorganization (Hu et al., 2025; Saleh et al., 2025). This marks a shift from storage-centric memory to process-oriented memory, in which the relevance of stored information is dynamically updated over time. Memory systems that support fine-grained updates recognize that personalization must operate at multiple levels, including episodic experience, user preferences, and behavioral patterns. MemOS (Li et al., 2025c) was among the first to formalize memory as a core system component, introducing a lifecycle management mechanism (MemCube) that enables dynamic memory scheduling, aging out obsolete facts while reinforcing relevant ones over long horizons. Similarly, Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) is a scalable memory-centric architecture that dynamically extracts, consolidates, and retrieves salient conversational information from ongoing interactions, supporting persistent, structured memory beyond raw document retrieval. Memobase focuses on extracting and maintaining structured user profiles and tagged memory records from chat interactions, serving as a scalable backend for personalized applications. Supermemory provides a unified memory API that builds structured relationships between facts to support persistent recall and relational context beyond simple vector proximity. Compared to existing benchmarks (Table 3), the differentiation of PERMA lies in the multi-dimensional decoupling of its evaluation. While LLMs and memory systems have improved in memory capacity, they still lack a fine-grained characterization of event-driven persona state evolution, which is essential for reflecting the mastery of user preferences. Furthermore, by integrating context noise and temporal probing, PERMA enables us to verify the coherence persona state within complex event streams, independent of mere interaction quality.

3. Preliminaries

To formally characterize the construction of a long-context, event-driven dialogue dataset, we establish a mathematical framework defining the constituent elements of the user profile and the temporal interaction sequence.

Definition 3.1.

Data Specification. Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} denote the set of users. For each user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U}, the user profile is defined as a triplet 𝒫u={𝒟u,ℐu,ℰu}\mathcal{P}_{u}=\{\mathcal{D}_{u},\mathcal{I}_{u},\mathcal{E}_{u}\} where 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} is the demographic profile, such as age and gender. ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} denotes the set of user interests, ℰu\mathcal{E}_{u} denotes the temporally ordered interaction events between the user and assistant.

Definition 3.2.

Interaction Event. An interaction event in ℰu\mathcal{E}_{u} at time step tt is defined as a tuple et=(τt,domt,𝒞t,Φt)e_{t}=(\tau_{t},\text{dom}_{t},\mathcal{C}_{t},\Phi_{t}), where τt∈{Emergence,Supplement,Task}\tau_{t}\in\{\textsc{Emergence},\textsc{Supplement},\textsc{Task}\} denotes event type:

  • •

    Emergence: The user’s first discovery of a domain, establishing initial preferences.

  • •

    Supplement: A follow-up interaction where preferences are refined, modified, or deepened.

  • •

    Task: A task-oriented user query probing the model’s integration of prior preferences.

domt⊆ℐu\text{dom}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{u} is the set of relevant domains involved in this event. 𝒞t=[(qt(1),at(1)),…,(qt(N),at(N))]\mathcal{C}_{t}=[(q_{t}^{(1)},a_{t}^{(1)}),\dots,(q_{t}^{(N)},a_{t}^{(N)})] represents the multi-turn dialogue content, consisting of NN turns of user queries qt(k)q_{t}^{(k)} and assistant responses at(k)a_{t}^{(k)}. Φt\Phi_{t} is the set of explicit or implicit preferences revealed during this event.

When τt=Task\tau_{t}=\textsc{Task}, Φt\Phi_{t} is empty and 𝒞t=[qt(1)]\mathcal{C}_{t}=[q_{t}^{(1)}]. This event serves as a checkpoint to evaluate the model’s response to preference-relevant queries (i.e. qt(1)q_{t}^{(1)}). A task can be Single-Domain if |domt|=1|\text{dom}_{t}|=1 or Multi-Domain if |domt|>1|\text{dom}_{t}|>1, with the latter requiring the joint synthesis of preferences across domains. Each task utilizes the current persona state as a user preference prior. Tasks are classified into three types based on their position in the interaction history:

  • •

    Type 1 (Zero-Memory): Evaluated at the onset of user interaction before relevant preferences are established.

  • •

    Type 2 (In-Time): Positioned immediately after all domain-relevant sessions in domt\text{dom}_{t} have occurred.

  • •

    Type 3 (Post-Intervention): Positioned after a series of sessions containing unrelated topics.

Definition 3.3.

Persona State. For a user uu, we define the persona state at time tt as a text representation 𝒮tu\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u} that synthesizes integrated user preferences and episodic memory derived from the concatenated dialogues 𝒢u,≤t={𝒞1,𝒞2,…,𝒞t}\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t}=\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}\} corresponding to historical events ℰu,≤t=(e1,e2,…,et)\mathcal{E}_{u,\leq t}=(e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{t}):

(1) 𝒮tu=f⁡({𝒞1,𝒞2,…,𝒞t}),\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u}=f(\{\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{C}_{t}\}),

where for memory systems, ff denotes an operator that aggregates the persona state by incorporating newly emerged or updated preferences from historical dialogues. In contrast, for standalone LLMs and vanilla RAG systems, ff reduces to an identity mapping over the raw interaction history. Unlike the static user profile 𝒫u\mathcal{P}_{u}, the persona state 𝒮tu\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u} evolves dynamically, reflecting incremental preference refinements and potential drift, thus enriching 𝒫u\mathcal{P}_{u} with fine-grained preference and behavioral details.

Definition 3.4.

Persona Consistency Objective. Given a sequence of historical events ℰu,≤t=(e1,…,et)\mathcal{E}_{u,\leq t}=(e_{1},\dots,e_{t}), where ete_{t} is a task event, which requires the agent to generate a response ata_{t} to the query qtq_{t} that maximizes alignment with the user’s evolved persona state extracted from the interaction dialogues 𝒢u,≤t\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t}. Formally, the model PP seeks to optimize the objective:

(2) a=arg⁡maxa′⁡P⁡(a′∣qt,𝒮tu)s.t.𝒮tu=f⁡(𝒢u,≤t),a=\arg\max_{a^{\prime}}\;P\big(a^{\prime}\mid q_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u}\big)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u}=f(\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t}),

where aa should satisfy the joint constraints of the demographic attributes in 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u} and the preference updates encapsulated in Φ1:t\Phi_{1:t}. That is, the agent should navigate multi-session and cross-domain history to synthesize relevant memory segments.

Definition 3.5.

Memory System. Compared to directly injecting historical interactions 𝒢u,≤t\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t} and user query qtq_{t} into a standalone LLM to generate a response aa, memory systems ℳ\mathcal{M} implement a dual-process mechanism composed of an ingestion operation (Add) and a retrieval operation (Search). Given the completed interaction sessions 𝒢u,≤t\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t} of user uu observed at timestamp tt, the system updates its internal persona state by Add:

(3) 𝒮tu←Add​(ℳ,𝒢u,≤t),\mathcal{S}^{u}_{t}\leftarrow\textsc{Add}(\mathcal{M},\mathcal{G}_{u,\leq t}),

where the ingestion process may involve indexing conversational history, extracting salient facts, or updating structured user persona state, such as a knowledge graph. Subsequently, for a user query qtq_{t}, the system retrieves a set of contextually relevant memory segments 𝐬t⊆𝒮tu\mathbf{s}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{S}_{t}^{u} by Search:

(4) 𝐬t←Search​(𝒮tu,ℳ,qt,k),\mathbf{s}_{t}\leftarrow\textsc{Search}(\mathcal{S}^{u}_{t},\mathcal{M},q_{t},k),

where kk denotes the number of retrieved items. The effectiveness of a memory system ℳ\mathcal{M} is reflected by the utility of 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} in answering user query qtq_{t}.

4. Methodology

In this section, we introduce PERMA. Rather than treating personalization as static preference recall, our framework models personalization as evolving preferences through an event-driven reconstruction of dialogue histories (Section 4.1). To better reflect real-world user-assistant interactions, Section 4.2 introduces two interaction variants by (1) injecting text variability based on common user prompt biases (Tian et al., 2025), (2) aligning query linguistic styles with real-world data. We evaluate downstream queries that do not explicitly trigger preference retrieval, thereby testing whether agents can proactively leverage stored information to integrate and enforce composite, cross-domain preferences (Section 4.3).

4.1. Event-Driven Dialogue Reconstruction

We construct dialogue histories based on interaction summaries from PersonaLens (Zhao et al., 2025b), which are grounded in authentic user profiles derived from the PRISM dataset (Kirk et al., 2024). These profiles span 20 distinct domains, ranging from Movies to Flights. We extend these concise summaries into long-horizon, consistent dialogue histories that capture the gradual emergence and iterative refinement of user preferences.

As illustrated in Figure 2 (a), we decompose each domain-level interaction summary into a sequence of chronological events, where each event corresponds to a coherent interaction session and remains consistent with the user profile. For each event in the timeline, we generate (1) an event description that defines the conversational scope and the key behavioral cues, (2) an interaction goal that specifies the intended dialogue outcome, and (3) a set of dependencies that determine the generation ordering among events. This event specification constrains dialogue generation to realize concrete behavioral signals, rather than vague conversational templates. During the generation, the agent is provided with user preference categories and the aforementioned context. Guided by event descriptions and objectives, the dialogue generation agent elaborates on the necessary preference details through either explicit user descriptions or implicit feedback.

4.1.1. Phase I: Timeline and Dialogue Generation

Given an interaction history summary ℋu\mathcal{H}_{u} provided by Personalens (Zhao et al., 2025b) and a user demographic profile 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u}, we employ a capable LLM (e.g., GPT-4o) as a high-level planner to construct an interaction timeline 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Formally, let fplanf_{\text{plan}} denote the LLM timeline planner. For each topic domain k∈ℐuk\in\mathcal{I}_{u}, the planner generates a domain-specific timeline conditioned on the corresponding historical summary ℋuk\mathcal{H}_{u}^{k}:

(5) 𝒯k=fplan​(𝒟u,k,ℋuk).\mathcal{T}_{k}=f_{\text{plan}}(\mathcal{D}_{u},k,\mathcal{H}_{u}^{k}).

We first prompt the model to categorize timeline entries into two types: Preference Emergence and Preference Supplement as introduced in Definition 3.2, thereby modeling iterative refinement over time. Each entry e^∈𝒯k\hat{e}\in\mathcal{T}_{k} is further associated with a detailed conversation description and cross-domain dependencies to facilitate inter-domain linkage.

Let 𝒯k={e^1,…,e^M}\mathcal{T}_{k}=\{\hat{e}_{1},\dots,\hat{e}_{M}\} denote the chronological sequence of MM timeline entries associated with user uu within the same domain kk. We iteratively generate a multi-turn dialogue 𝒞m\mathcal{C}_{m} for each timeline entry e^m\hat{e}_{m} using an LLM PgP_{g}, conditioned on the user profile 𝒟u\mathcal{D}_{u}, interest categories ℐu\mathcal{I}_{u} and the previously generated dialogue history 𝒢u,m−1k={𝒞1k,…,𝒞m−1k}\mathcal{G}^{k}_{u,m-1}=\{\mathcal{C}^{k}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}^{k}_{m-1}\}.

(6) 𝒞mk,Φmk∼Pg(⋅∣𝒟u,ℐu,e^t,𝒢u,m−1k)\mathcal{C}^{k}_{m},\Phi^{k}_{m}\sim P_{g}(\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{u},\mathcal{I}_{u},\hat{e}_{t},\mathcal{G}^{k}_{u,m-1})

where Φm\Phi_{m} represents any new preferences that emerged or updated during this session. For the initial preference emergence entry within a domain, where no prior interactions exist, the entry itself serves as the starting point. We validate generated results with human experts and an LLM-based verification pipeline. The final event is constructed by concatenating the timeline entry e^\hat{e} with the corresponding dialogue 𝒞mk\mathcal{C}^{k}_{m} and preferences, i.e., em=concat​(e^m,𝒞mk,Φmk)e_{m}=\textbf{concat}(\hat{e}_{m},\mathcal{C}^{k}_{m},\Phi^{k}_{m}).

After generating all events across domains, we construct a global timeline 𝒯final\mathcal{T}_{\text{final}} by interleaving the domain-specific timelines {𝒯k}k=1K\{\mathcal{T}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. This aggregation respects explicitly defined cross-domain dependencies and strictly enforces chronological order according to the parsed timestamps, with a unified time index tt across all events.

4.1.2. Phase II: Task Insertion

To evaluate memory utilization at varying temporal depths, we inject evaluation tasks into 𝒯final\mathcal{T}_{\text{final}} using a timestamp-based insertion strategy that probes the lifecycle of preference development. For a task event et​(τt=Task)e_{t}(\tau_{t}=\textsc{Task}) associated with relevant domains d​o​mt⊂ℐudom_{t}\subset\mathcal{I}_{u}, we establish three types of evaluation checkpoints (Definition 3.2). As shown in Figure 2 (b), we place Type 1 (Zero-Memory) tasks at the onset of the timeline, before any relevant events occur, serving as a non-personalized control to separate the parametric bias of the agent from persona-based answers. Type 2 task is placed right after the final events of relevant domains to evaluate the integration of the entire trajectory. Additionally, to quantify robustness against forgetting and contextual interference, we construct Type 3 tasks by positioning tasks at the conclusion of the global timeline. This checkpoint follows a series of intervening sessions involving unrelated domains. By comparing the performance delta between Type 2 and Type 3, we can effectively measure the agent’s resilience over a long horizon.

4.2. Alignment with Real-World Interactions

In event-driven persona state modeling, the inherent noise and disfluencies of real-world interactions present significant hurdles. For example, user utterances can be vague, and preferences are often fragmented across multiple messages. While prior research (Zhao et al., 2025a; Jiang et al., 2025a) has introduced preference updates across multiple sessions, we aim to incorporate a broader spectrum of text variability observed in human prompts for LLM (Tian et al., 2025), as well as individual idiolects.

4.2.1. Text Variability Injection.

In natural interactions, user inputs frequently contain vague expressions, inconsistent preferences, or context switch, as illustrated in Table 2. Such phenomena challenge personalized memory agents not only in retrieving relevant information but also in integrating histories and composing accurate persona-state signals.

However, synthetic text is often standardized and lacks variability, even when using a high temperature for generation (West and Potts, 2025). To bridge this gap, we introduce a controlled noise injection process during dialogue generation. Specifically, we perturb user turns with contextually grounded in-session noise that preserves conversational plausibility. Building upon the original dialogue-generation prompt and extracted preferences Φ\Phi, we augment the generation process by providing a noise specification 𝒵\mathcal{Z} that describes the intended perturbation type (e.g., omitted references, context switch, or inconsistent preferences). We also generate examples conditioned on 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, which are incorporated as one-shot in-context demonstrations (Brown et al., 2020) in noise specification to guide the dialogue generation agent.

Formally, similar to Equation 6, let e^m\hat{e}_{m} denote the current timeline entry in domain kk, and 𝒢u,m−1n​o​i​s​e={𝒞1n​o​i​s​e,…,𝒞m−1n​o​i​s​e}\mathcal{G}^{noise}_{u,m-1}=\{\mathcal{C}^{noise}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{C}^{noise}_{m-1}\} the previously generated noisy dialogues. Let 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m} denote the noise specification sampled for event eme_{m}. The noisy dialogue generation process can be expressed as:

(7) 𝒞mnoise∼Pg(⋅∣𝒟u,Φm,e^m,𝒢u,m−1n​o​i​s​e,𝒵m).\mathcal{C}_{m}^{\text{noise}}\sim P_{g}\big(\cdot\mid\mathcal{D}_{u},\Phi_{m},\hat{e}_{m},\mathcal{G}^{noise}_{u,m-1},\mathcal{Z}_{m}\big).

Compared to the Clean setting, the conditioning variable 𝒵m\mathcal{Z}_{m} steers the user turn construction toward vague or misleading patterns, all while preserving semantic alignment with the underlying persona state. By substituting the original turns in ℰ\mathcal{E} with 𝒞mn​o​i​s​e\mathcal{C}^{noise}_{m}, we derive the perturbed event sequence ℰn​o​i​s​e\mathcal{E}^{noise}, and keep the global timeline 𝒯final\mathcal{T}_{\text{final}} unchanged. Under these conditions, the model is expected to maintain a stable persona state 𝒮tu\mathcal{S}^{u}_{t}, perform context-aware retrieval and resist irrelevant turns.

4.2.2. Linguistic Alignment.

Real-world user inputs exhibit individual idiolects. In contrast, synthetic conversations often follow standardized templates, which simplifies retrieval and artificially inflates evaluation scores, especially when the generator and the agent share the same underlying model. To prevent models from exploiting overt lexical cues, we construct user prompts to mimic the authentic linguistic patterns observed in real-world interaction corpora.

Specifically, we randomly sample real-world conversations from WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024) for each user prompt in the Clean setting, and instruct an LLM to align the linguistic style of the synthetic user prompt with the real data, while preserving the underlying user intent. In addition, we interleave WildChat data as irrelevant distractors within the global timeline, extending the total context up to 128k tokens. This design challenges models to infer persona states from diverse, individualized linguistic patterns across long-context sessions, thereby increasing the tasks’ complexity.

Together, text variability and linguistic alignment ensure that our evaluation extends beyond idealized preference recall. Instead, PERMA probes the model’s capacity to maintain coherent persona-state tracking even when confronted with pervasive ambiguity and authentic linguistic variability.

4.3. Evaluation Protocol

To systematically evaluate persona state tracking across temporal depths and contextual complexities, PERMA adopts a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol. This protocol integrates temporally controlled task insertion to evaluate cross-session evolution, positional probing within long contexts to assess retrieval robustness, and comprehensive metrics that capture both factual correctness and persona consistency.

4.3.1. Evaluation Checkpoints (Type 1/2/3).

Checkpoint tasks are strategically inserted into the global timeline to probe distinct stages of persona-state development. Type 1 tasks are positioned before any domain-relevant events occur, serving as a zero-memory baseline to disentangle the agent’s parametric bias from its persona-based responses. Type 2 tasks are introduced immediately following the emergence of all relevant domains to assess peak recall. Finally, Type 3 tasks are placed at the end of the global timeline, after multiple intervening sessions. At this stage, the persona state is fully developed but heavily occluded within a substantially longer and noisier history.

4.3.2. Contextual Position Probing.

In addition to temporal stage control, we probe evaluation tasks at varying positions within contexts (e.g., 10%–100% event segments of the histories). By measuring performance as a function of this relative distance, we analyze how different personalized memory agents balance retrieval efficiency and contextual scanning. This positional probing provides a fine-grained view of how persona state utilization degrades or stabilizes as context length increases.

4.3.3. Metrics and Assessment Dimensions.

Evaluation is conducted along three primary dimensions: task performance, memory fidelity and efficiency.

Task Performance

We evaluate system performance in both one-shot and interactive settings. In the former, we employ Multiple-Choice Question (MCQ) to measure selection accuracy (MCQ Acc.). The MCQ options are generated by ablating three core aspects: (i) Task Completion, indicating the fulfillment of defined goals; (ii) Preference Consistency, ensuring responses are grounded in long-term preferences without hallucinating unsupported inferences; and (iii) Informational Confidence, identifying whether the model maintains a decisive stance without uncertainty (see Figure 18 for details). By enumerating all binary combinations of three aspects, we yield eight distinct evaluation categories.

To better approximate real-world usage, we introduce an interactive evaluation using an LLM-based user simulator (see Figure 16 for the prompt). The simulator is granted access to the ground-truth dialogue history and relevant preference annotations. It terminates the session by outputting “TERMINATE” only when the task is successfully completed while satisfying all user preferences. Otherwise, it provides supplementary feedback, and the dialogue continues.

We report the success rate at Turn=1 and Turn≤\leq2. Compared to the one-shot setting, the interactive evaluation not only assesses open-text responses but also distinguishes suboptimal memory (resolvable with a single feedback round) from low-quality memory (requiring extensive clarification). Interactions are capped at a maximum of 10 turns. We report task Completion representing the percentage of tasks successfully terminated within this interaction limit, serving as a measure of overall system reliability.

Memory Fidelity

We calculate the BERT-f1 between the retrieved context and ground-truth dialogues, complemented by a Memory Score (see Figure 19) derived via an “LLM-as-a-judge” protocol. This protocol evaluates task coverage, accuracy, and preference consistency. Specifically, this scoring mechanism penalizes the omission of critical persona facets while rewarding concise, task-relevant retrievals that enhance downstream utility.

Efficiency

We calculate Context Token to measure the average number of memory tokens consumed per query. To quantify memory retrieval efficiency within long-context environments, we also record the Search Duration. In the interactive setting, User Token tracks the total tokens generated by the user simulator, capturing the communicative overhead and degree of preference clarification required to resolve a task.

5. Experiments

5.1. Experiment Setup

5.1.1. Datasets and Evaluation Metrics.

We utilize the datasets detailed in Section 4.1 & 4.2, which incorporate event-driven preferences, text variability, and linguistic alignment. The evaluation setup is described in Section 4.3.

5.1.2. Personalized Memory Approaches.

We evaluated a range of personalized memory approaches on PERMA, categorized into two paradigms: 1) standalone LLMs, 2) agents with RAG and memory systems.

Standalone LLMs.

In this setting, the full dialogue history is provided to the model as input without any retrieval mechanism or memory compression. We evaluate both reasoning models and chat models, investigating their capabilities in synthesizing preferences across multiple domains and fragmented sessions.

  • •

    MiniMax-M2.511 1 https://www.minimax.io/news/minimax-m25: A large-scale reasoning model specializing in zero-shot reasoning over extensive contexts.

  • •

    GLM-5/GLM-4.7-Flash (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026): GLM-5 is a reasoning model tested by consuming the complete interaction history, and GLM-4.7-Flash provides fast inference while maintaining solid reasoning ability.

  • •

    Kimi-K2.5 (Team et al., 2026): A reasoning model designed for large input windows, evaluated without external retrieval.

  • •

    Qwen3-32B/Qwen2.5-72B/Qwen2.5-14B-1M (Yang et al., 2025): Reasoning and chat models from the Qwen family, offering strong general-purpose reasoning and long-context comprehension.

  • •

    Llama3.3-70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024b): 70B model in the Llama3 known for general reasoning and instruction-following capabilities.

  • •

    Gemini2.5-Flash (Comanici et al., 2025): An instruct model designed to deliver strong generation performance with low latency.

  • •

    GPT-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024): A variant of the GPT-4 tailored for efficient conversational reasoning and general tasks.

Agents with RAG and Memory Systems.

To evaluate retrieval-augmented approaches, we implement several RAG and structured memory systems with GPT-4o-mini as the backbone response generator.

  • •

    RAG (Gao et al., 2023): A standard retrieval-augmented generation baseline using BGE-M3 (Chen et al., 2023) as the dense retriever to retrieve top-kk relevant dialogue chunks, which are then concatenated as evidence for generation.

  • •

    MemOS (Li et al., 2025c) introduces a memory operating system for LLMs that manages heterogeneous memory types through structured memory units (MemCube) and provides lifecycle scheduling, storage, and retrieval mechanisms.

  • •

    Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) introduces a scalable memory layer that automatically extracts, compresses, and persistently stores salient user information, enabling dynamic long-term personalization across sessions.

  • •

    LightMem (Fang et al., 2025) proposes a lightweight memory-augmented framework inspired by cognitive memory models, organizing information into short- and long-term memory stages with efficient compression.

  • •

    Memobase22 2 https://www.memobase.io/ provides a persistent memory management system that organizes user preferences across sessions.

  • •

    EverMemOS (Hu et al., 2026a) proposes a long-term conversational memory architecture that organizes interaction histories into episodic traces and semantic memory structures, enabling reconstructive retrieval for long-horizon reasoning.

  • •

    Supermemory33 3 https://supermemory.ai/research uses hierarchical, semantically structured memory for retrieval and long-term persona modeling.

5.1.3. Implementation Details.

For standalone LLMs, we invoke their APIs. For memory systems, we evaluate both cloud-based and locally deployed frameworks. MemOS (v1), Mem0 (v2), Memobase (v1), and Supermemory (v4) are accessed via online cloud services for Add and Search operations. EverMemOS and Lightmem are deployed locally using MongoDB (Tao et al., 2024) for information storage and Milvus (Wang et al., 2021) as the vector database. For RAG and memory systems, we perform semantic retrieval by fetching the top-1010 chunks as the default setting, where each chunk in RAG is defined as a single user-assistant pair for embedding.

5.1.4. Human Validation.

During event construction, rigorous human validation is performed to ensure that all user preferences are explicitly or implicitly manifested within the dialogue histories (see Section 4.1 and Figure 2). This process guarantees the foundational integrity of the dataset. Furthermore, we conduct a human evaluation of the MCQ options to verify their quality. Given the ground-truth dialogue history, human experts achieve an impressive 97.75% accuracy on the tasks, demonstrating high alignment between the task objectives and the provided dialogue data.

Beyond the MCQ tasks, human experts evaluate additional content generation aspects using the criteria protocol detailed in Figure 20. Specifically, we assess whether the constructed events accurately cover the goals and descriptions specified in the timeline entries (as described in Section 4.1.1), yielding a near-perfect score of 1.99/2. Regarding the injection of text variability, experts find that 98% of the modifications successfully adhere to the designated noise types, confirming the efficacy of our text variability injection process.

5.2. Overall Performance

The empirical performance of all evaluated models across single- and multi-domain tasks, under both Clean and Noise scenarios, is detailed in Tables 4 through 7. We analyze the persona state across temporal depth and compare different models and memory systems from multiple perspectives, including MCQ task accuracy (MCQ Acc.), memory fidelity (BERT-f1, Memory Score), Search efficiency (Search Tokens and Duration), and interactive success rates (Completion, User Token usage, Turn = 1, Turn≤\leq2).

5.2.1. Performance on Clean Interactions

Table 4 and Figure 3 present a comprehensive comparison of standalone LLMs and personalized memory agents under the Clean setting. From these results, we derive the following observations:

  1. (1)

    Reasoning Models vs. Chat Models. Reasoning models demonstrate a clear advantage in maintaining persona state consistency. Specifically, Kimi-K2.5 achieves the highest MCQ Acc. (0.882), followed by Qwen3-32B (0.870) and Gemini2.5-Flash (0.870). It suggests that superior base model capabilities are essential for synthesizing user preferences and episodic information from interaction dialogue histories.

  2. (2)

    Performance and Efficiency of Memory Systems. Memory systems present a compelling alternative for resource-constrained applications. Notably, Supermemory and Lightmem compress the context tokens to fewer than 300, representing a reduction of over 99% raw content. However, we find these two systems sacrifice task fulfillment for context compression, underperforming even compared to vanilla RAG. Among the evaluated methods, MemOS achieves an effective balance of the performance-efficiency trade-off, obtaining the highest MCQ Acc. (0.811) and Memory Score (2.27) while consuming fewer Context Token (709.1) than vanilla RAG (828.8).

    Additionally, EverMemOS attains a high Completion rate (0.846), it incurs substantial search latency when deployed locally (16s), which limits its applicability under time-sensitive scenarios. In contrast, locally deployed vanilla RAG spends only 16ms on retrieval and obtains competitive success rates (0.830).

    Furthermore, the interactive evaluation—captured by Turn=1 and Turn≤\leq2 metrics—reveals distinct behavioral patterns among the memory systems. MemOS achieves the highest Turn=1 success rate (0.548), indicating that its retrieved persona state more effectively enables agents to provide preference-satisfied responses in a one-shot manner. In contrast, while Memobase and Lightmem lag in immediate resolution, they lead in Turn≤\leq2 performance (Memobase: 0.830 and Lightmem: 0.813). This suggests that while the responses provided by them are initially suboptimal, their persona states possess strong recovery capabilities, allowing agents to reach the desired response with just a single round of user feedback. Conversely, Mem0 exhibits the lowest Turn≤\leq2 success rate, implying that its persona state often requires extensive user involvement and multiple clarification rounds to resolve the task.

  3. (3)

    RAG vs. Memory Systems. RAG achieves the highest BERT-f1 score (0.849), indicating that most key information can be successfully retrieved via dense semantic matching. However, because these retrieved dialogue fragments are often disjointed and unorganized, the downstream model struggles to reconstruct a coherent persona state. In contrast, advanced memory systems (e.g., MemOS) effectively link related information and integrate temporal structures into a unified persona. This structured representation substantially alleviates the cognitive and synthesis burden on the response-generating LLM. Consequently, memory systems significantly outperform RAG, as evidenced by superior MCQ Acc. and Completion rates.

  4. (4)

    Performance across Different Temporal Depths. Figure 3 demonstrates the robustness of persona tracking by comparing performance across three types of evaluation checkpoints (Types 1–3). We utilize Type 1 accuracy as a non-personalized baseline, representing the model’s zero-shot capability. Across all evaluated systems, accuracy consistently declines from Type 2 to Type 3, suggesting that increased dialogue depth amplifies memory interference and undermines coherent persona maintenance. Memory Scores for Memobase and Mem0 exhibit a pronounced drop in the Type 3, indicating a strong recency bias where late-stage inputs break long-term persona maintenance. In contrast, MemOS achieves the most stable performance throughout the interaction, demonstrating architectural robustness against a long interaction history.

5.2.2. Comparative Analysis: Clean vs. Noisy Settings

To assess the robustness of different architectures under realistic interaction conditions, we further extend our evaluation to a Noisy setting. Specifically, we inject text variability as in-session noise while maintaining the original user intent (see Section 4.2). By jointly analyzing the results reported in Table 4 and Table 5, together with the visualization in Figure 4, we identify several critical findings.

  1. (1)

    Robustness of Standalone LLMs against Text Variability. Many standalone LLMs maintain comparable performance when in-session noise is introduced. As shown in Figure 4 (1), Gemini 2.5-Flash demonstrates superior handling of noisy contexts, maintaining high accuracy (0.879). In contrast, while Kimi-K2.5 excels in Clean scenarios (0.882), its performance drops to 0.865. It is thus more susceptible to such distraction compared to Gemini.

  2. (2)

    Noise as a Semantic Catalyst for Memory Systems. Several memory systems exhibit improved performance in the noisy setting. Further investigation shows that in-session noise acts as an internal conflict that inadvertently emphasizes preference information, thereby facilitating more effective extraction. This is consistent with the findings reported in PrefEval (Zhao et al., 2025a). An example is MemOS, whose retrieval volume nearly doubles from 709.1 tokens (Clean) to 1486.7 tokens (Noise). This expanded context provides a more detailed description of user preferences, leading to an increase in Memory Score (2.27→\rightarrow2.38) and MCQ Acc. (0.811→\rightarrow0.853).

5.2.3. Comparative Analysis: Single Domain vs. Multi-Domain.

In this section, we extend our evaluation to the multi-domain queries to examine the agents’ capability in synthesizing information cross-domains (Table 6). The transition from single to multi-domain query reveals a significant performance gap. Our findings are:

  1. (1)

    Overall Performance of Multi-Domain Queries. As shown in Table 6, all memory system based agents experience a pronounced decline in performance compared to the single-domain tasks. It is particularly evident in interactive metrics, where the success rate at the first attempt (Turn=1) has declined significantly, meanwhile the average User Token count has increased.

  2. (2)

    Cross-Domain Interference and Evaluation Limitations. As shown in Figure 5 (1), in the single-domain tasks, standalone LLMs may not perform worse at Type 3 checkpoints with longer dialogue histories compared with Type 2 checkpoints. This phenomenon suggests that the presence of irrelevant tokens does not necessarily obstruct the LLM’s ability to retrieve and utilize task-relevant information. Instead, the model appears capable of filtering or tolerating moderate noise when the contextual structure remains simple and domain boundaries are clear.

    However, this robustness does not generalize to multi-domain tasks (Figure 5 (2)). As noise increases, performance deteriorates consistently across most LLMs, indicating the difficulty of synthesizing information across domains in long context. In particular, Llama3.3-70B exhibits a sharp performance drop, reflecting susceptibility to irrelevant information when contexts and dialogues are interleaved.

    Beyond this degradation, we observe a clear divergence between option accuracy MCQ Acc. and interactive performance as well as Memory Score in memory systems. While memory system-based agents maintain relatively stable accuracy (Table 6, Figure 6 (2)), both their memory scores and response quality decline substantially under the same conditions. This indicates that selecting the correct option from predefined candidates is considerably easier than generating a reasoned answer through multi-step inference. Moreover, since the memory score primarily reflects retrieval precision, successful recall of key preferences can enable downstream reasoning to compensate for irrelevant context, partially hiding degradation in memory quality. These findings highlight a limitation of prior evaluations: option accuracy alone is insufficient to characterize the effectiveness of memory in multi-domain tasks.

  3. (3)

    Recall Robustness of Memory Systems vs. RAG. As illustrated in Figure 6, the effectiveness of memory systems varies across different evaluation checkpoints. While the introduction of irrelevant information reduces retrieval precision, memory systems maintain high recall of task-relevant preference signals due to their structured persona-state representation. In contrast, standard RAG relies on semantic similarity-based retrieval, making it more susceptible to interference from irrelevant context and consequently leading to a pronounced performance decline.

  4. (4)

    Retrieval Expansion and Structural Limitations. To better support multi-domain queries that require broader evidence aggregation, we expand the number of retrieved items from 10 to 20. However, this expansion leads to performance degradation in most memory system, as illustrated in Figure 7. Since these memory systems rely on compressed persona-state representations, the inclusion of excessive irrelevant information may introduce noise that interferes with downstream reasoning. In contrast, standard RAG benefits significantly from increased retrieval depth. Since RAG retrieves semantic fragments that may lack contextual completeness, retrieving more candidates improves coverage of missing situational details. These findings reveal that current memory systems rely on fixed retrieval memory segments and lack the ability to adapt retrieval precision to varying task difficulty and information demands.

5.2.4. Performance Dynamics in Multi-Domain Noise Scenarios

In the multi-domain noise environment, the performance of standalone LLMs diverges significantly from memory systems-based agents, revealing critical insights into reasoning capacity and retrieval efficiency.

  1. (1)

    Performance of Standalone LLMs. As indicated in Table 7, standalone LLMs with enhanced reasoning capability, such as Kimi-K2.5, demonstrate substantial resilience to text variability and the complexity of multi-domain queries, maintaining a robust MCQ Acc. of 0.930. It suggests that advanced reasoning is a pivotal driver in stable preference formation, especially navigating environments with high contextual entropy. In contrast, chat models such as Llama3.3-70B, suffer a marked performance degradation, with accuracy falling to 0.656. highlighting a significant susceptibility to complex tasks with high contextual entropy.

  2. (2)

    Performance Changes in Interactive Scenarios. Figure 8 shows the performance fluctuations of memory system-based agents compared to standalone LLMs in the presence of noise. Notably, memory systems exhibit higher sensitivity, particularly during interactive tasks where response accuracy drops after noise is introduced. This degradation is more pronounced than that observed in the single-domain setting shown in Figure 4. These results suggest that while current memory systems decompose queries (Ma et al., 2023) and rerank retrieved memory, they still struggle to integrate and properly order information across domains when dealing with noisy environments.

    Finally, taking a holistic view of Figure 9, we observe that, when comparing performance between the Type 3 and Type 2 positions, memory systems generally maintain stable Turn=1 performance and remain largely robust to token-level noise introduced by irrelevant dialogue. Moreover, relative to the no-memory baseline (Type 1), they achieve consistent and steady improvements. However, compared to the single-domain tasks, the disparity among different memory systems becomes more pronounced in the multi-domain evaluation, particularly at the Type 2 position, suggesting that memory systems differ in their sensitivity to cross-domain complexity.

  3. (3)

    Efficiency Changes in Multi-domain Noisy Scenarios. Efficiency metrics further show that the introduction of noise leads to a substantial increase in computational overhead. As shown in Table 7, the Search Duration of EverMemOS rises to 26s, significantly higher than in the clean multi-domain setting, suggesting that semantic noise increases the difficulty of retrieval and preference synthesis. In contrast, Lightmem maintains a consistently low latency of 9.1ms, indicating better scalability under noisy conditions.

5.3. Further Analysis

5.3.1. Performance under Linguistic Style-aligned Long Contexts

To evaluate the limits of standalone LLMs and memory systems, we extend our experiments to a long context setting with an average length of 116k tokens. This setup simulates large-scale interaction histories and stress-tests models’ ability to maintain effective memory under extreme context lengths. Following the pipeline described in Section 4.2.2, we align the user queries of the Clean setting with real-world conversational styles and populate the context with authentic dialogue segments sampled from WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024).

  1. (1)

    The impact of stylistic interference and token-level noise. In the single-domain task performance shown in Figure 8, comparing the base metrics (Clean setting in Table 4) to the style-aligned results shows that the performance of most memory systems remains largely unchanged. This suggests that, as long as preference information and task requirements are preserved, variations in linguistic style have a limited impact on long-context understanding.

    In contrast, the introduction of substantial irrelevant token noise reveals divergent behaviors between standalone LLMs and memory systems. For GPT-4o-mini, the model fails to respond under long dialogue inputs. Similarly, Qwen2.5-14B-1M, despite being fine-tuned on ultra-long contexts, exhibits a performance decline (from 0.766 to 0.716). Memory systems, however, maintain stable performance, highlighting their robustness to token-level noise that is less relevant to personal preference.

  2. (2)

    Persona State Consistency in Long-Context Multi-Domain Settings. The multi-domain setting exposes the fragility of most memory systems. While MemOS is the top-performing system with an MCQ Acc. of 0.764, and its interaction performance also shows improvement compared to the Clean version (Turn=1: 0.306 →\rightarrow 0.331; Turn≤\leq2: 0.592 →\rightarrow 0.637). Systems like Supermemory and Mem0 witness a performance collapse (falling below 0.60). This divergence suggests that maintaining persona consistency over 100k+ tokens requires resilient state tracking rather than simple semantic matching. Further analysis of memory content in Appendix B shows that, although these systems improve token efficiency relative to MemOS, they primarily record episodic memories and fail to abstract and consolidate specific facts or preferences.

  3. (3)

    User Variability and Long-Context Degradation. Figure 11 reveals that performance is non-uniform across different user profiles, highlighting the diversity present in the dialogues. As the context length increases, Figure 11(2) illustrates a catastrophic performance degradation beyond the 60% position (approximately 73k tokens), where the base model (GPT-4o-mini) reaches the limits of its effective context processing capability and ultimately fails at the 100% mark. In contrast, memory systems such as MemOS exhibit remarkable stability. By transforming the global long-context reasoning problem into a persona-state matching task, MemOS effectively bypasses the physical context window limitations of the underlying LLM, thereby sustaining high accuracy even at extreme context length.

  4. (4)

    Robustness under Positional Probing. Compared to prior work that evaluates preference at a fixed position, we continuously assess the model’s ability to maintain multiple preferences across diverse positions through event-driven persona state evolution. In contrast to the global query evaluation in Figure 11 (2), the results in Table 9 specifically focus on queries associated with previously emerged domain events, measuring the variation in MCQ Acc. across positional checkpoints from 10% to 100% depth. While some memory systems experience slight performance variance within the median depth range (30%–60%), MemOS maintains superior and stable accuracy, surpassing even the Qwen2.5-14B-1M. This stability suggests that its indexing mechanism successfully handles semantic overlap and retrieval interference in dense context segments.

5.3.2. Single-domain vs. Multi-domain Robustness

Figure 12 provides a comprehensive comparison across different settings, highlighting a performance divergence between single-domain and multi-domain tasks. In single-domain tasks (Figure 12 (left)), the style-aligned long-context (Long) setting generally acts as a performance bottleneck for most memory systems, such as Memobase, where accuracy falls below the Clean setting. This indicates that extended sequences introduce interference during retrieval in focused tasks. In multi-domain tasks (Figure 12 (righ)), the trends diverge: while RAG and Supermemory exhibit performance degradation under the Long setting, MemOS and Memobase instead show improvements over their Clean settings. This suggests that certain architectures benefit from the structured data distribution in style-aligned contexts, which helps resolve cross-domain dependencies.

5.3.3. Topic-Specific Adaptation and Domain Expertise

Table 10 reveals clear domain-specific performance variations across different approaches. Large-scale models such as Kimi-K2.5 achieve the strongest results in structured domains like Finance (0.914) and Messaging (0.980), where task requirements are relatively stable. Within the memory systems, MemOS narrows the gap between plug-in memory-based agents and vanilla models, particularly in the Shopping (0.889) and Travel (0.856) domains, demonstrating improved utilization of historical preferences. In contrast, a consistent performance drop is observed in the Media and Restaurant domains across all evaluated models. These domains typically involve more dynamic and frequently updated user preferences, making them inherently more challenging. This suggests that memory should not function solely as a storage of historical interactions and preferences, but should be actively leveraged to guide future responses by transforming accumulated preference signals into informative priors for inference.

6. Conclusion

In this work, we introduce a benchmark that shifts the evaluation of personalized memory agents from static preference recall to longitudinal persona consistency. By constructing temporally ordered interaction events, we propose an event-driven framework, PERMA, for assessing standalone LLMs and memory systems under text variability and real-world linguistic alignment. Our experiments in single- and multi-domain tasks, as well as long-context settings, reveal that most memory-based systems outperform RAG by linking related interactions into a persistent persona state. This advantage becomes more pronounced in high-entropy settings, where memory systems demonstrate greater robustness and achieve 50×\times to 300×\times higher token efficiency than vanilla long-context models. Notably, while standalone LLMs exhibit severe performance degradation when context exceeds their window sizes, memory systems remain stable by reducing long-range reasoning to structured persona state matching. Despite these gains, performance degradation under multi-domain transitions and conflicting signals reveals a sensitivity to context complexity, further highlighting the necessity of PERMA. Overall, our findings suggest that, while memory enhances robustness, achieving truly personalized agents requires moving beyond static retrieval toward task-aware, dynamic memory management capable of filtering noise and maintaining long-term coherence, ultimately enabling lifelong companionship.

Appendix A Prompt

To establish a realistic foundation for evaluation, the framework utilizes data construction prompts that simulate the evolution of user preferences. By leveraging TIMELINE_GENERATION in Figure 13, the system generates interaction timelines, modeling how user interests emerge and deepen. These timelines are then transformed into naturalistic dialogues via the DIALOGUE_GENERATION prompts in Figure 15, which guide the LLMs to reveal preferences through feedback or corrections, thereby mirroring the ambiguity of real-world interactions.

Building upon this data, the framework transitions to a dynamic interactive simulation driven by the User simulator. As the interaction unfolds, the USER_FEEDBACK_PROMPT in Figure 16 provides the user’s responses, enabling the agent to provide adaptive feedback. This mechanism allows the simulated user to clarify intent or correct the assistant based on history, creating a test of the assistant’s ability to maintain consistency and adapt to user guidance in real-time.

Finally, to quantify agent performance, the module implements a standardized “LLM-as-a-Judge” evaluation. We score the assistant’s responses on quality and personalized memory (EVAL_MEMORY_SCORE in Figure 19). Crucially, the system assesses memory precision, verifying the retrieval of details against ground truth. OPTION_GENERATION_PROMPT in Figure 18 synthesizes challenging multiple-choice questions with options that are plausible but intentionally misaligned with user preferences or facts, thereby testing the agent’s discriminative ability in noisy environments.

Appendix B Case Study

In this section, we present a case study comparing the retrieved memory of different systems to provide a clearer horizontal evaluation. As illustrated in Table 11–12, we can intuitively observe the retrieved memory results of various systems for the same query: MemOS categorizes memory into three distinct dimensions—episodic facts, explicit preferences, and implicit preferences—utilizing a parallel retrieval mechanism that effectively addresses the three categories of challenges inherent in preference-driven scenarios; meanwhile, Mem0, Memobase, and EverMemOS prioritize the concatenation of episodic memories, which makes them better suited as personal assistants for querying historical records but leaves them relatively weak in preference extraction and processing; conversely, Supermemory leans toward highly abstracted preference extraction but fails to reconstruct the specific details of relevant events along the timeline.
